verses.text: What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found?
For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.
For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.
Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.
Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness.
How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.

And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also:
And the father of circumcision to them who are not of the circumcision only, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had being yet uncircumcised.
For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect:
Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.

Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed; not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham; who is the father of us all,
( As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.
Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations; according to that which was spoken, So shall thy seed be.
And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb:
He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God;
And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.
And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness.
Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him;
But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead;
Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.

summary: Paul argues his case from the one figure no Jewish reader could dismiss: "Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh." If Abraham "were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God" — and the scripture itself settles the matter, for "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness." The verb governs everything that follows. Wages are owed, not given: "to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt." But righteousness comes to "him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly." David sings the same blessedness, "unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works" — "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered" — "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin." Paul then presses the question of timing, which is really the question of who may be included: "Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also?" The answer is chronological and decisive: "Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision." Abraham was reckoned righteous before he bore the covenant mark, and "he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised," precisely "that he might be the father of all them that believe." He is father also "to them who are not of the circumcision only, but who also walk in the steps of that faith." The inheritance follows the same logic: "the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith," since if heirship ran through law then "faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect," and law by itself "worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression." So "it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed." Paul closes with a portrait of what such faith actually looked like. Abraham stood "before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were." He "against hope believed in hope"; "being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead" at "about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb"; he "staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God," "being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform." "And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness." The record is not antiquarian: "it was not written for his sake alone," but "for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification."
takeaways: Paul's argument turns on a date, not a debate. Genesis credits Abraham with righteousness before the covenant mark is given, so Paul can ask "How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision?" and answer from the record itself: "Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision." The sequence, not merely the principle, makes Gentile inclusion structural rather than a later concession.

Circumcision is not dismissed but reclassified. It is "the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised" — a visible ratification of something already given, not the instrument that produced it. That distinction between what confers and what confirms shapes every later Christian argument about signs, marks, and sacraments.

The faith Paul praises is not bare assent to a proposition but sustained trust against evidence. Abraham "considered not his own body now dead" nor "the deadness of Sara’s womb"; he "staggered not at the promise" and was "fully persuaded" — and the object of that trust is defined theologically as "God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were." Faith here is measured by the God it holds onto.

Grace and certainty are linked, not opposed. "Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed." A promise contingent on law-keeping would be as unstable as the keepers; resting it on grace is what makes it "sure" and what makes it extend beyond one people.

The chapter ends by making Abraham's story a template for Christian faith with a specific content: righteousness is imputed "if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead." The same God who quickens the dead womb raises the crucified Son, "delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification" — resurrection is not an appendix to justification but part of its ground.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 15:5-6 — he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness
crossRefs.why: This is the verse Paul quotes as his whole proof text, spoken when God brought Abram outside to number the stars. Reading it in place shows that the reckoning came in response to a promise about descendants Abraham could not produce, which is exactly the reading Paul gives it in "who against hope believed in hope."

crossRefs.label: Genesis 17:9-14 — it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you
crossRefs.why: Circumcision is instituted here, chapters after the reckoning of righteousness in Genesis 15, which is the chronological gap Paul exploits when he insists it was "Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision." The passage also shows how weighty the sign was in itself, so that Paul is reordering rather than trivializing it.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 32:1-2 — Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity
crossRefs.why: Paul's second witness, cited as "David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works." The psalm's setting is confession of sin and the relief of forgiveness, which grounds Paul's claim that this blessedness belongs to "him that justifieth the ungodly" rather than to the already-worthy.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 3:6-14 — they which be of faith, the same are the children of Abraham
crossRefs.why: Paul makes the identical argument to a different crisis, again quoting the Genesis reckoning and again concluding that Gentiles enter the promise without taking on the law. Read alongside Romans 4 it shows this is not an occasional rhetorical move but Paul's settled reading of Abraham as the pattern of all who believe.

crossRefs.label: James 2:18-26 — was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac?
crossRefs.why: James cites the same Genesis text about Abraham believing God but draws it toward a faith that is "made perfect" by works and is dead without them. The two passages together set the terms of the entire justification debate, since each apostle appeals to Abraham and to the same verse while addressing different errors.

crossRefs.label: Romans 5:1-11 — being justified by faith, we have peace with God
crossRefs.why: Chapter 5 draws the immediate consequence of the Abraham argument, moving from how righteousness is reckoned to what it produces: peace, access, hope, and "the love of God" shed abroad in the heart. It shows Paul does not leave justification as a bare verdict but continues at once into the transformed life it opens.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading holds that when God "counted" and "imputed" righteousness to Abraham, the reckoning was effective rather than merely notional: God's declaration accomplishes what it declares, so the justified are genuinely made righteous by grace poured into them, not left unrighteous while treated as if they were not. On this reading the "works" excluded in "if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory" are works that would generate a boast and a debt — including the works of the law and circumcision that dominate the chapter's argument — and not the obedience that flows from grace already received, which Paul himself commends in those who "walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters typically read the reckoning language as forensic and declarative: righteousness is credited to the believer's account as a standing before God rather than infused as a quality within, and justification is therefore distinct from the sanctification that follows it. The strongest textual footing is the accounting vocabulary Paul chooses — "reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt" — together with "to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly," and above all the negative form in "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin," which describes a non-reckoning rather than an interior change. Both traditions affirm that justification is entirely God's gift, that no one may boast before God, and that a justified life must issue in real obedience; the disputed point is whether Paul's reckoning language names the gift of a new interior righteousness or a verdict credited from outside.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the faith Paul praises here as inherently living and self-committing rather than bare intellectual assent, and therefore denies that this chapter teaches justification by faith alone in the sense of a faith that could stand isolated from love and obedience. The chapter's own portrait supports the point: Abraham "staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief," was "strong in faith, giving glory to God," and was "fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform" — a trust that reoriented his whole life and, in the Genesis narrative Paul is expounding, moved him to act. Notably the word "alone" never appears beside faith in this chapter.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters hold that Paul does exclude every human work from the ground of justification, since he sets working and believing in strict opposition — "to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt" — and specifies righteousness imputed "without works," not merely without ceremonial works. On this reading faith is indeed never alone in the justified person, and produces obedience necessarily, but it justifies alone, because any contribution of works would convert grace into wages and reintroduce the boast Paul denies. The two readings largely agree on what the Christian life must look like and differ on whether the obedience that faith produces is part of the ground of justification or its inevitable fruit.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in "he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith" a pattern for sacramental theology: God attaches visible signs to his grace, and those signs genuinely seal and convey what they signify rather than merely picturing it. The chapter is read as establishing the priority of grace and faith over the sign without reducing the sign to an optional badge, since Abraham did in fact receive it at God's command, and baptism is understood as the corresponding seal under the new covenant.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters commonly read the same phrase as confirming that the sign follows and attests a righteousness already received by faith, and therefore that no rite can be the instrument of justification — the whole force of "Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision" is that Abraham was righteous before he was marked. Traditions differ among themselves on how much the sacraments convey, but generally emphasize that they are seals of a prior grace received through faith rather than causes of it. Both readings agree that the sign is God-given and not optional for those to whom it is commanded, and that it points beyond itself to the faith it ratifies.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
